claim: Planar cell polarity (PCP) controls convergent extension and axis elongation in all vertebrates.
source: Planar cell polarity (PCP) controls convergent extension and axis elongation in all vertebrates.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that draws from established scientific consensus in the field.

claim: Asymmetric localization of PCP proteins is central to their function.
source: Although asymmetric localization of PCP proteins is central to their function, we understand little about PCP protein localization during convergent extension.
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge in the PCP field.

claim: PCP protein enrichment is tightly correlated with actomyosin-driven contractile behavior of cell-cell junctions.
source: We observed asymmetric enrichment of PCP proteins, but more interestingly, we observed tight correlation of PCP protein enrichment with actomyosin-driven contractile behavior of cell-cell junctions.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's observations and quantitative analysis.

claim: The turnover rates of junctional PCP proteins correlate with the contractile behavior of individual junctions.
source: Moreover, we found that the turnover rates of junctional PCP proteins also correlated with the contractile behavior of individual junctions.
evidence: This finding is supported by FRAP experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: All dynamic relationships between PCP proteins and junction behavior were disrupted when PCP signaling was manipulated.
source: All these dynamic relationships were disrupted when PCP signaling was manipulated.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data using Xdd1 and Pk2-ΔPΔL manipulations.

claim: Cell intercalation is thought to be driven by extension of mediolaterally directed cellular protrusions.
source: Cell intercalation, in turn, is thought to be driven by multiple subcellular behaviors, including extension of mediolaterally directed cellular protrusions (e.g. [Keller and Hardin, 1987; Shih and Keller, 1992])
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Cell intercalation is thought to be driven by active shrinkage of mediolaterally oriented cell-cell junctions.
source: Cell intercalation, in turn, is thought to be driven by multiple subcellular behaviors, including extension of mediolaterally directed cellular protrusions (e.g. [Keller and Hardin, 1987; Shih and Keller, 1992]) and active shrinkage of mediolaterally oriented cell-cell junctions (e.g. [Bertet et al., 2004; Blankenship et al., 2006]).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Mediolaterally directed cellular protrusions and junction shrinking likely work in concert during cell intercalation.
source: More recent data suggest that these two subcellular behaviors likely work in concert (Sun et al., 2017; Williams et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to recent work.

claim: The junction shrinking mechanism for cell intercalation was initially described in Drosophila.
source: The junction shrinking mechanism for cell intercalation was initially described in Drosophila (Bertet et al., 2004; Blankenship et al., 2006)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to foundational work in Drosophila.

claim: Junction shrinking has been identified in both epithelial and mesenchymal cells in vertebrates.
source: The junction shrinking mechanism for cell intercalation was initially described in Drosophila (Bertet et al., 2004; Blankenship et al., 2006) and was subsequently identified in both epithelial and mesenchymal cells in vertebrates (Lienkamp et al., 2012; Nishimura et al., 2012; Shindo and Wallingford, 2014; Trichas et al., 2012; Williams et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to vertebrate studies.

claim: Junction shrinkage is accompanied by pulsed actomyosin contractions that are restricted to or enriched at mediolaterally oriented cell-cell junctions.
source: In all tissues examined by live imaging, junction shrinkage is accompanied by pulsed actomyosin contractions that are restricted to or enriched at mediolaterally oriented cell-cell junctions and absent from or less common at the junctions perpendicular to the anterior-posterior axis (Bertet et al., 2004; Blankenship et al., 2006; Shindo and Wallingford, 2014; Williams et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to multiple live imaging studies.

claim: In Drosophila, pair-rule genes and Toll receptors are crucial regulators of polarized actomyosin.
source: In Drosophila, pair-rule genes and Toll receptors are crucial regulators of polarized actomyosin (Paré et al., 2014; Zallen and Wieschaus, 2004)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Drosophila studies.

claim: Homologous genes to Drosophila pair-rule genes and Toll receptors do not appear to be involved in vertebrate convergent extension.
source: In Drosophila, pair-rule genes and Toll receptors are crucial regulators of polarized actomyosin (Paré et al., 2014; Zallen and Wieschaus, 2004), but homologous genes do not appear to be involved in vertebrates.
evidence: This is a comparative statement based on knowledge of the field.

claim: The most well-characterized regulator of mediolateral cell intercalation in vertebrates is the Planar Cell Polarity (PCP) signaling system.
source: Instead, the most well-characterized regulator of mediolateral cell intercalation in vertebrates is the Planar Cell Polarity (PCP) signaling system (Butler and Wallingford, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: PCP signaling controls cell intercalation during gastrulation and neural tube closure in frogs, fish, and mice.
source: Indeed, PCP signaling controls cell intercalation during gastrulation and neural tube closure in frogs, fish, and mice, and mutations in PCP genes are now a well-defined genetic risk factor for human neural tube birth defects (NTDs) (De Marco et al., 2014; Juriloff and Harris, 2012; Wallingford et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to multiple studies across different model organisms.

claim: Mutations in PCP genes are a well-defined genetic risk factor for human neural tube birth defects (NTDs).
source: Indeed, PCP signaling controls cell intercalation during gastrulation and neural tube closure in frogs, fish, and mice, and mutations in PCP genes are now a well-defined genetic risk factor for human neural tube birth defects (NTDs) (De Marco et al., 2014; Juriloff and Harris, 2012; Wallingford et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to human genetics studies.

claim: Cell polarity is imparted by asymmetric enrichment of the core PCP proteins.
source: One fundamental principle of PCP signaling is that cell polarity is imparted by asymmetric enrichment of the core PCP proteins (Butler and Wallingford, 2017; Strutt and Strutt, 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: In Drosophila, the Prickle (Pk) and Van Gogh (Vangl) proteins act in concert on one side of the cell, and Dishevelled and Frizzled act on the complementary side.
source: As shown first in Drosophila, the Prickle (Pk) and Van Gogh (Vangl) proteins act in concert on one side of the cell, and Dishevelled and Frizzled act on the complementary side (Axelrod, 2001; Bastock et al., 2003; Strutt, 2001; Tree et al., 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to foundational Drosophila studies.

claim: FRAP studies in Drosophila have shown that patterns of PCP protein enrichment are driven by planar polarization of the junctional turnover kinetics of PCP proteins.
source: Interestingly, FRAP studies in Drosophila have shown that these patterns of enrichment are driven by planar polarization of the junctional turnover kinetics of PCP proteins, underscoring the dynamic nature of the PCP signaling system (Strutt et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to FRAP studies in Drosophila.

claim: Similar patterns of PCP protein enrichment and turnover have been reported in vertebrate epithelia.
source: Similar patterns of enrichment and turnover have been reported in vertebrate epithelia (Butler and Wallingford, 2015; Chien et al., 2015; Shi et al., 2016)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to vertebrate studies.

claim: Complementary, asymmetric domains of PCP protein enrichment have been described during vertebrate convergent extension.
source: For example, complementary, asymmetric domains of PCP protein enrichment have been described during vertebrate CE (Ciruna et al., 2006; Jiang et al., 2005; McGreevy et al., 2015; Ossipova et al., 2015; Roszko et al., 2015; Yin et al., 2008)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to multiple vertebrate studies.

claim: PCP proteins are required for the junction shrinking behaviors that contribute critically to cell intercalation.
source: This gap in our knowledge is critical, because recent work demonstrates that PCP proteins are required for the junction shrinking behaviors that contribute critically to cell intercalation (Lienkamp et al., 2012; Nishimura et al., 2012; Shindo and Wallingford, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to recent work.

claim: Prickle2 (Pk2) and Vangl2 were dynamically enriched specifically at shrinking cell-cell junctions and depleted from elongating junctions during cell intercalation.
source: Strikingly, we find that in addition to expected patterns of spatial asymmetry, PCP protein enrichment is tightly linked to cell-cell junction behavior: Prickle2 (Pk2) and Vangl2 were dynamically enriched specifically at shrinking cell-cell junctions and depleted from elongating junctions during cell intercalation.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's time-lapse imaging and quantitative analysis.

claim: FRAP analysis revealed that patterns of PCP protein enrichment reflected differences in the kinetics of protein turnover at shrinking versus non-shrinking junctions.
source: FRAP analysis revealed that these patterns of enrichment reflected differences in the kinetics of protein turnover at these sites.
evidence: This is supported by FRAP experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: Pk2 enrichment was temporally and spatially correlated with planar polarized oscillations of junctional actomyosin enrichment.
source: Moreover, Pk2 enrichment was temporally and spatially correlated with planar polarized oscillations of junctional actomyosin enrichment.
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse imaging data showing co-localization and correlation of Pk2 and Myl9.

claim: Studies in Xenopus consistently prefigure similar results in mammalian systems.
source: We characterized PCP protein dynamics in the neural plate of Xenopus, as studies in this animal consistently prefigure similar results in mammalian systems yet provide exceptional views of dynamic cell biological processes.
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge about the utility of Xenopus as a model system.

claim: Dishevelled and Frizzled function in both PCP and canonical Wnt signaling.
source: Because Dishevelled and Frizzled function in both PCP and canonical Wnt signaling, their roles are more difficult to interrogate
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge about these proteins.

claim: Prickle and Vangl act solely in PCP signaling.
source: so we focused instead on Prickle and Vangl, which act solely in PCP signaling
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge about these proteins.

claim: Prickle and Vangl are required for convergent extension and neural tube closure in vertebrates, including Xenopus.
source: so we focused instead on Prickle and Vangl, which act solely in PCP signaling and are required for CE and neural tube closure in vertebrates, including Xenopus (Darken et al., 2002; Goto et al., 2005; Goto and Keller, 2002; Kibar et al., 2001; Takeuchi et al., 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Previous work suggests that Prickle and Vangl localize to the anterior face of cells in the Xenopus neural plate.
source: Previous work suggests that Prickle and Vangl localize to the anterior face of cells in the Xenopus neural plate (Ossipova et al., 2015)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Overexpression of PCP proteins has a well-documented effect on PCP signaling.
source: Because overexpression of PCP proteins has a well-documented effect on PCP signaling, we used titration experiments to empirically determine the lowest possible dose of mRNA that allowed imaging in the Xenopus neural plate.
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge in the field.

claim: GFP-Vangl2 displayed a strong asymmetric bias to anterior cell faces under low mRNA dose conditions.
source: Under these conditions, GFP-Vangl2 displayed a strong asymmetric bias to anterior cell faces (Figure 1A)
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: At slightly higher doses of injected mRNA, low levels of Vangl2 could be observed at the posterior faces as well.
source: while at slightly higher doses of injected mRNA, low levels of Vangl2 could be observed at the posterior faces as well (not shown), consistent with previous reports (Ossipova et al., 2015; Roszko et al., 2015).
evidence: This observation is consistent with previous reports cited.

claim: GFP-Pk1 did not display asymmetric enrichment in the Xenopus neural plate.
source: Core PCP proteins are encoded by multi-gene families, and despite the reported role of Prickle1 in convergent extension, GFP-Pk1 did not display asymmetric enrichment in our hands (not shown).
evidence: This is a negative result from the authors' experiments.

claim: GFP-Prickle2 was strongly enriched anteriorly in the Xenopus neural plate.
source: However, GFP-Prickle2 (Butler and Wallingford, 2015) was strongly enriched anteriorly (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: GFP-Pk2 was restricted to the apicolateral cell junctional regions.
source: GFP-Pk2 was also restricted to the apicolateral cell junctional regions, as expected (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Knockdown experiments confirmed that Pk2 was physiologically relevant for convergent extension and neural tube closure in Xenopus.
source: Knockdown experiments confirmed that Pk2 was physiologically relevant for convergent extension and neural tube closure in Xenopus (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by morpholino knockdown experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: GFP-Vangl2 strongly co-localized with RFP-Pk2 in double-labeling experiments.
source: In double-labeling experiments, GFP-Vangl2 strongly co-localized with RFP-Pk2 (Figure 1A, Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1A and Video 1.

claim: GFP-Pk2 was significantly enriched at V-junctions as compared to T-junctions.
source: We found that GFP-Pk2 was significantly enriched at V-junctions as compared to T-junctions (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: There was a significant correlation between GFP-Pk2 pixel intensity and junction angle, with higher enrichment along more mediolaterally oriented junctions.
source: In a more granular view of the data, we observed a significant correlation between GFP-Pk2 pixel intensity and junction angle, with higher enrichment along more mediolaterally oriented junctions (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: In many systems, disruption of any one core PCP protein leads to loss of polarized enrichment of the others.
source: To test these quantification schemes, we took advantage of the fact that in many other systems, disruption of any one core PCP protein leads to loss of polarized enrichment of the others.
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge in the PCP field.

claim: Xdd1 is a well-defined, PCP-specific dominant negative of Dvl2.
source: Xdd1 is a well-defined, PCP-specific dominant negative of Dvl2 (Sokol, 1996; Wallingford et al., 2000)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Xdd1 disrupts convergent extension of the neural tube in Xenopus.
source: Xdd1 is a well-defined, PCP-specific dominant negative of Dvl2 (Sokol, 1996; Wallingford et al., 2000) that disrupts convergent extension of the neural tube in Xenopus (Wallingford and Harland, 2001; Wallingford and Harland, 2002)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Xdd1 expression severely disrupted Prickle2 asymmetries in the neural plate.
source: we found that Xdd1 expression severely disrupted Prickle2 asymmetries in the neural plate using both ensemble and individual metrics (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 1B,C.

claim: A deletion construct of Pk2 lacking the PET and LIM domains (Pk2-ΔPΔL) disrupted PCP in Xenopus multiciliated cells.
source: To extend this analysis, we explored Pk2 signaling by expressing a deletion construct lacking the PET and LIM domains (Pk2-ΔPΔL), as this construct disrupted PCP in Xenopus multiciliated cells and an equivalent deletion of Pk1 disrupts CE (Butler and Wallingford, 2015; Takeuchi et al., 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: An equivalent deletion of Pk1 disrupts convergent extension.
source: To extend this analysis, we explored Pk2 signaling by expressing a deletion construct lacking the PET and LIM domains (Pk2-ΔPΔL), as this construct disrupted PCP in Xenopus multiciliated cells and an equivalent deletion of Pk1 disrupts CE (Butler and Wallingford, 2015; Takeuchi et al., 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Pk2-ΔPΔL strongly disrupted axis elongation in Xenopus.
source: We found that Pk2-ΔPΔL strongly disrupted axis elongation in Xenopus (Figure 1—figure supplement 3)
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Pk2-ΔPΔL severely disrupted the planar asymmetry of co-expressed wild-type Pk2-GFP in the neural plate.
source: and also severely disrupted the planar asymmetry of co-expressed wild-type Pk2-GFP in the neural plate (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 1B,C.

claim: The neural plate of Xenopus consists of two cell layers, an outer epithelial layer and a deeper mesenchymal layer.
source: Curiously, the neural plate of Xenopus consists of two cell layers, an outer epithelial layer and a deeper mesenchymal layer (Schroeder, 1970).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Cell intercalation of the deep mesenchymal cells in the Xenopus neural plate has been characterized.
source: While cell intercalation of the deep mesenchymal cells has been characterized (Elul et al., 1997; Keller et al., 1992)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The behaviors of the overlying epithelial cells in the Xenopus neural plate have not been characterized.
source: While cell intercalation of the deep mesenchymal cells has been characterized (Elul et al., 1997; Keller et al., 1992), the behaviors of the overlying epithelial cells have not.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in the literature.

claim: It is the outer epithelial cells that display the robust patterns of PCP protein localization.
source: This distinction is not trivial, because it is the outer epithelial cells that display the robust patterns of PCP protein localization described above.
evidence: This is an inference based on the authors' observations.

claim: Neural tube closure spans roughly 6 hours in Xenopus.
source: Neural tube closure spans roughly 6 hr in Xenopus, starting with the shaping of the neural tube at last gastrula stages, followed by the progressive elevation and apposition of the neural folds (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Individual cell trajectories during neural tube closure closely resembled those of previous studies.
source: This approach allowed assessment of tissue-level morphogenetic changes in the neural plate, as well as individual cell trajectories, which closely resembled those of previous studies ((Figure 2B; Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and see [Keller et al., 1992]).
evidence: This is supported by cell tracking data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1, and comparison to previous work.

claim: Tracking of cell clusters revealed extensive intercalations that were mediolaterally biased, resulting in convergence and extension.
source: Moreover, our tiling approach provided sufficient magnification to quantify the discrete behaviors of individual cells, and tracking of cell clusters revealed extensive intercalations that were mediolaterally biased, resulting in convergence and extension (Figure 2C, Video 3).
evidence: This is supported by cell tracking data shown in Figure 2C and Video 3.

claim: Cell intercalations in the neural plate were associated with T transitions characterized by preferential contraction of junctions aligned in the mediolateral axis (T1-T2 transition).
source: Cell intercalations in the neural plate were associated with so-called T transitions, which are characterized by preferential contraction of junctions aligned in the mediolateral axis (T1-T2 transition) (Figure 3A,a')
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3A,a'.

claim: T transitions are followed by elongation of new junctions perpendicularly along the anteroposterior axis (T2-T3 transition).
source: followed by elongation of new junctions perpendicularly along the anteroposterior axis (T2-T3 transition)(Figure 3a', a'')(Bertet et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3a', a'' and citation to previous work.

claim: Mediolaterally oriented V-junctions preferentially shrank, while the perpendicular T-junctions elongated.
source: As above, we first quantified these behaviors at the ensemble level and found that mediolaterally oriented V-junctions preferentially shrank, while the perpendicular T-junctions elongated (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: There was a significantly positive correlation between junction angle and change in junction length, with V-junctions preferentially shrinking along the mediolateral axis and T-junctions elongating perpendicularly.
source: Moreover, when we plotted the change in the length of cell-cell junctions against the average angle of that junction for all cells examined (n > 250), we observed a significantly positive correlation; V-junctions preferentially shrank along the mediolateral axis and T-junctions elongated perpendicularly (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The orientation of shrinking and growing junctions remained fairly constant, changing on average only 5 (±4) degrees over the course of measurement.
source: Importantly, the orientation of shrinking and growing junctions in this analysis remained fairly constant, changing on average only 5 (±4) degrees over the course of measurement, and no junctions shifted by more than 20 degrees.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of junction angles over time.

claim: V-junctions separate anteroposterior (AP) neighbors and T-junctions separate mediolateral (ML) neighbors.
source: Thus, in general, V-junctions separate anteroposterior (AP) neighbors and T-junctions separate mediolateral (ML neighbors).
evidence: This is an inference based on the orientation data.

claim: Planar polarized formation and resolution of multicellular rosettes were observed in the Xenopus neural plate.
source: Finally, we also observed planar polarized formation and resolution of multicellular rosettes (Figure 3D–F), as have been described in other epithelia (Blankenship et al., 2006; Lienkamp et al., 2012; Trichas et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3D–F and citations to previous work.

claim: Expression of Xdd1 elicited a tissue level defect in the medially directed movement of the neural folds.
source: Using the mosaic approach described above, we found that expression of Xdd1 elicited the expected tissue level defect in the medially directed movement of the neural folds (Figure 4A, magenta nuclei indicate Xdd1 expressing cells).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Xdd1 expression significantly disrupted planar polarized junction shrinking, eliminating the strong correlation between junction angle and junction shrinkage or growth.
source: Analysis of individual cell behaviors in these embryos revealed that Xdd1 expression significantly disrupted planar polarized junction shrinking, eliminating the strong correlation between junction angle and junction shrinkage or growth (Figure 4B, compare with Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 4B compared to Figure 3C.

claim: Uncoupling of junction behavior from orientation by Xdd1 was associated with reduced junction shrinkage generally, and a reduction in the number of productive T transitions.
source: This uncoupling of junction behavior from orientation was associated with reduced junction shrinkage generally, and a reduction in the number of productive T transitions (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The few productive T transitions observed after Xdd1 expression were significantly slowed.
source: In fact, even the few productive T transitions that were observed were significantly slowed (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: During neural plate shaping stages (12-14), the majority of neural epithelial cells in control embryos exhibited a shift from an anteroposterior orientation to a mediolateral orientation.
source: Finally, these defects in cell intercalation behavior had a profound impact on cell shape. During neural plate shaping stages (12-14), the majority of neural epithelial cells in control embryos exhibited a shift from an anteroposterior orientation to a mediolateral orientation (Figure 4E, green)
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Xdd1 expressing cells maintain their alignment in the anteroposterior axis during neural plate shaping stages.
source: while Xdd1 expressing cells maintain their alignment in the anteroposterior axis (Figure 4E, blue).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Xdd1 expressing cells actually increased their length-to-width ratios along the AP axis.
source: In fact, these cells actually increased their length-to-width ratios along the AP axis (not shown)
evidence: This is mentioned as an observation from the authors' data.

claim: Genetic mutation of PCP genes in zebrafish elicits a similar spectrum of cell shape and orientation defects.
source: Notably, genetic mutation of PCP genes in zebrafish also elicits similar spectrum of cell shape and orientation defects (Roszko et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to zebrafish studies.

claim: Disruption of Prickle function by expression of the dominant-negative Pk2-ΔPΔL elicited the same spectrum of defects as Xdd1.
source: Finally, disruption of Prickle function by expression of the dominant-negative Pk2-ΔPΔL elicited the same spectrum of defects (Figure 4C,D, pink; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 4C,D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The accumulation of Pk2 was junction-specific, displaying overt changes in intensity precisely at tricellular junctions.
source: First, we noted that the accumulation of Pk2 was junction-specific, displaying overt changes in intensity precisely at tricellular junctions (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: GFP-Pk2 was dynamically enriched at shrinking junctions but depleted from elongating junctions.
source: Moreover, we found that GFP-Pk2 was dynamically enriched at shrinking junctions but depleted from elongating junctions (Figure 5A)
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Dynamic enrichment of Pk2 might not simply reflect the junction's spatial orientation.
source: suggesting that dynamic enrichment of Pk2 might not simply reflect the junction's spatial orientation (e.g. to V- vs. T-junctions).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that similarly oriented junctions can have different Pk2 levels.

claim: Even when adjacent junctions share a similar orientation, the GFP-Pk2 intensity at these junctions frequently differed substantially.
source: This notion was support by the observation that even when adjacent junctions share a similar orientation, the GFP-Pk2 intensity at these junctions frequently differed substantially (Videos 4 and 5).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Videos 4 and 5.

claim: Among similarly oriented junctions, shrinking is associated with increasing levels of Pk2-GFP intensity, and elongation with decreasing Pk2-GFP.
source: Even among these similarly oriented junctions, shrinking is associated with increasing levels of Pk2-GFP intensity, and elongation with decreasing Pk2-GFP (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Similar results to Pk2 were obtained for Vangl2.
source: Similar results were obtained for Vangl2 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Changes in GFP-Pk2 fluorescence intensity showed a strong and highly significant correlation with corresponding changes in junction length.
source: To quantify these observations, we plotted the changes in GFP-Pk2 fluorescence intensity against corresponding changes in junction length, and we observed a strong and highly significant correlation (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Changes in Vangl2 fluorescence intensity showed a strong and highly significant correlation with corresponding changes in junction length.
source: Similar results were observed with Vangl2 (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: A generic membrane marker (FP-caax) showed a tendency to increase as junctions shrink, but this increase was modest and the correlation was far weaker than that observed for PCP proteins.
source: To explore this idea, we examined a generic membrane marker (FP-caax) and found that while it did show a tendency to increase as junctions shrink, this increase was modest and the correlation was far weaker than that observed for PCP proteins (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Even when normalized against the membrane marker, the intensities of GFP-Vangl2 and GFP-Prickle2 still displayed strong and significant correlations with junction shrinkage.
source: Importantly, even when normalized against the membrane marker to account for changes in membrane-FP in the same junctions, the intensities of GFP-Vangl2 and GFP-Prickle2 still displayed strong and significant correlations with junction shrinkage (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The enrichment of Pk2 and Vangl2 is governed both by the reciprocal interaction of each individual pair of neighboring cells and is intricately linked to the behavior of the shared junction between them.
source: Together, these data suggest that the enrichment of Pk2 and Vangl2 is governed both by the reciprocal interaction of each individual pair of neighboring cells and is intricately linked to the behavior of the shared junction between them.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation data presented.

claim: FRAP studies have demonstrated that polarized PCP protein turnover is planar polarized in other cell types.
source: FRAP studies have demonstrated that polarized PCP protein turnover is planar polarized in other cell types (Butler and Wallingford, 2015; Chien et al., 2015; Shi et al., 2016; Strutt et al., 2011)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous FRAP studies.

claim: Both Pk2 and Vangl2 displayed striking differences in turnover kinetics at shrinking versus non-shrinking junctions, with significantly less recovery (i.e. higher stable fraction) at shrinking junctions.
source: Both Pk2 and Vangl2 displayed striking differences in turnover kinetics at shrinking versus non-shrinking junctions, with significantly less recovery (i.e. higher stable fraction) for both Vangl2 and Prickle2 at shrinking junctions compared to non-shrinking junctions (Figure 7B,C).
evidence: This is supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 7B,C.

claim: The stable fraction of both Pk2 and Vangl2 correlated significantly with changes in junction length: more rapidly shrinking junctions displayed higher stable fractions of junctional PCP proteins.
source: Moreover, when we integrated these FRAP data with time-lapse analysis of cell behaviors, we found that the stable fraction of both proteins correlated significantly with changes in junction length: more rapidly shrinking junctions displayed higher stable fractions of junctional PCP proteins (Figure 7D,E).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 7D,E.

claim: The overall accumulation of Prickle2 and Vangl2 at shrinking junctions parallels the increased stability of these proteins at these sites.
source: Thus, the overall accumulation of Prickle2 and Vangl2 at shrinking junctions parallels the increased stability of these proteins at these sites
evidence: This is an inference based on the FRAP and localization data.

claim: PCP protein trafficking plays a key role in the coordination of cell-cell junction shrinkage.
source: and together, these data suggest a key role for PCP protein trafficking in the coordination of cell-cell junction shrinkage.
evidence: This is an inference based on the turnover kinetics data.

claim: Time-lapse imaging in Drosophila first demonstrated that cell intercalation by junction shrinkage is accompanied by pulsed accumulations of actomyosin at V-junctions.
source: Time-lapse imaging in Drosophila first demonstrated that cell intercalation by junction shrinkage is accompanied by pulsed accumulations of actomyosin at V-junctions (Bertet et al., 2004; Fernandez-Gonzalez et al., 2009; Rauzi et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Drosophila studies.

claim: Actomyosin pulsing during junction shrinkage is independent of PCP signaling in Drosophila.
source: While this process is independent of PCP signaling in Drosophila
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge about Drosophila.

claim: Similar actomyosin pulses have been observed during PCP-dependent junction shrinking in mesenchymal cells of the Xenopus gastrula mesoderm.
source: similar actomyosin pulses have been observed during PCP-dependent junction shrinking in mesenchymal cells of the Xenopus gastrula mesoderm (Shindo and Wallingford, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Static analyses of Xenopus, chicks and mice indicate that actomyosin is enriched at mediolaterally oriented junctions.
source: Static analyses of Xenopus, chicks and mice also indicate that actomyosin is enriched at mediolaterally oriented junctions (McGreevy et al., 2015; Nishimura et al., 2012; Williams et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Myl9-GFP showed a strong enrichment at V-junctions as compared to T-junctions.
